Q: Wireless Debugging not working in Android Studio on MAC A:

I have tried multiple answers here. This is what worked for me:

  • wifi connection, make sure it is not randomized mac on wifi settings (mac, phone)

  • make sure adb tools is installed on mac

  • close android studio (yes ik but for some reason, protocol fault occurs due to multiple adb being open)

  • start adb start-server, adb pair <ip>:<port> <pairing code> from wifi debugging settings on android, it will be successfully connected on cli

  • now open android studio, the device is connected via wifi debugging

Q: Label at the specific UNIX timestamp not on the same bar between different charts A:

When passing the UNIX time for the x argument using xloc.bar_time, it must match the time of the bar, which is the start time. Otherwise, the label is placed on the first bar over the specified UNIX time.

A good way to visualize this is with the following snippet:

// DEBUG
labelColor = switch
   time == unix    => color.green 
   time < unix     => color.gray
   time > unix     => color.maroon
label.new(bar_index, 0, str.format_time(time, "yyyy-MM-dd\nHH:mm:ss\nZ", "UTC"), style = label.style_label_up, yloc = yloc.belowbar, color = color.new(labelColor, 50))

Q: Lightweight test management for tracking manual + automated test runs without heavy overhead? A:

When we evaluated lightweight test management, the criteria that mattered most were speed and navigability under load. How fast can someone log a run, find last release coverage, or answer “did we test this before?” If those answers take more than a few clicks, people stop using the tool and you’re back to tribal knowledge.

Second was how well it coexists with automation. Not replacing CI dashboards, just linking builds to intent. Being able to see automated and manual coverage side by side without duplicating structure helped a lot, especially during releases and incident reviews.

We looked at Qase and TestRail too and had the same reaction, powerful but heavier than we needed. Tools like Tuskr stood out more for low overhead and fast run logging. Less about feature depth, more about staying out of the way so engineers actually keep it updated.

Long term, the tools that last are the ones that minimize maintenance. Structure that helps discovery without demanding constant curation. Once upkeep feels like a job, the system decays no matter how strong the feature list is.

Q: How do I properly decorate a `classmethod` with `functools.lru_cache`? A:

The selected answer is totally correct but adding another post. If you want to bind the cache storages to each classes, instead of sharing the single storage to all its subclasses, there is another option methodtools

import functools
import methodtools


class K:
    @classmethod
    @functools.lru_cache(maxsize=1)
    def mthd(cls, s: str):
        print('functools', s)
        return s

    @methodtools.lru_cache(maxsize=1)  # note that methodtools wraps classmethod
    @classmethod
    def mthd2(cls, s: str):
        print('methodtools', s)
        return s


class L(K):
    pass


K.mthd('1')
L.mthd('2')
K.mthd2('1')
L.mthd2('2')

K.mthd('1')  # functools share the storage
L.mthd('2')
K.mthd2('1')  # methodtools doesn't share the storage
L.mthd2('2')

Then the result is

$ python example.py
functools 1
functools 2
methodtools 1
methodtools 2
functools 1
functools 2
